source_text: ὡδί πη πάλιν· «Καὶ ταῦτα φάγεσθε ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἐν τοῖς ὕδασι· πάντα ὅσα ἐστὶν αὐτοῖς πτερύγια καὶ λεπίδες ἐν τοῖς ὕδασι, καὶ ἐν ταῖς θαλάσσαις, καὶ ἐν τοῖς χειμάῤῥοις, ταῦτα φάγεσθε· καὶ πάντα ὅσα οὐκ ἔστιν αὐτοῖς πτερύγια, οὔτε λεπίδες ἐν τοῖς ὕδασι, καὶ ἐν ταῖς θαλάσσαις, καὶ ἐν τοῖς χειμάῤῥοις, ἀπὸ πάντων ὧν ἐρεύγεται τὰ ὕδατα καὶ ἀπὸ πάσης ψυχῆς ζώσης ἐν τῷ ὕδατι, βδέλυγμά ἐστι, καὶ βδελύγματα ἔσονται ὑμῖν. Ἀπὸ τῶν κρεῶν αὐτῶν οὐκ ἔδεσθε, καὶ τὰ θνησιμαῖα αὐτῶν βδελύξεσθε, καὶ πάντα ὅσα οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν αὐτοῖς πτερύγια οὔτε λεπίδες τῶν ἐν τοῖς ὕδασι, βδέλυγμα τοῦτό ἐστιν ὑμῖν.» {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ἀλλ' ἥτις ποτέ ἐστιν ἔν γε δὴ τούτοις ἡ διαφορὰ, κατὰ θεωρίαν δὴ λέγω τὴν πνευματικὴν, φράσαις ἂν αὐτός. Συνίημι γὰρ οὔτι που μάλα ἐγώ. {ΚΥΡ.} Πάνυ μὲν οὖν· ἐρῶ γὰρ, ὡς ἔνι, μεταπλάττων ἐπὶ τὸ ἐμφανὲς τὰ ὡς ἐν τρόπῳ παραδειγμάτων τῷ νόμῳ παρειλημμένα· ὅσα μὲν γὰρ τῶν ἐν τοῖς ὕδασι πρὸς τοῦ πάντων Δημιουργοῦ τῷ τῶν ἰχθύων εὖ μάλα πεπλαστούργηται νόμῳ, ταῖς τῶν πτερυγίων ἐκβολαῖς οἱονείπως ἀεὶ διερέττοντα, τὴν οἵπερ ἂν ἕλοιντο τυχὸν ὡς εὐσθενῆ καὶ εὐδρομωτάτην ποιοῦνται κίνησιν. Καὶ ἡλίου μὲν θερμὴν ἄνωθεν ἐνιέντος τοῖς ὕδασι τῆς ἀκτῖνος τὴν προσβολὴν, ἀνανήχεται, καὶ μονονουχὶ καὶ αὐτῶν τῶν ὑδάτων ἀναθρώσκειν ἀποτολμᾷ, τὸ κάτω μένειν ἀεὶ παραιτούμενα, διεξοίχεται δὲ ῥᾳδίως καὶ τῶν θηρώντων τὰ λῖνα. Τά γε μὴν οὐκ ἐν λεπίσι καὶ πτερυγίοις, ἤγουν ἐν ἐλύτροις ὄντα σκληροῖς, καὶ ὀστράκῳ τῷ συμφυεῖ κατημφιεσμένα, ἥκιστα μὲν οἶδε τὸ ἄνω, εἰσδύεται δὲ τὴν εἰς τὸ κάτω πόαν ἀεὶ, καὶ τοῖς ἰλυώδεσι τῶν τόπων ἐμφιλοχωρεῖ. Ἀδρανῆ τέ ἐστι καὶ εὐάλωτα, καὶ τοῖς ἅπαξ τεθεαμένοις, ἱδρῶτος δίχα ληπτά. Καὶ λόγος μὲν ἐπ' ἐκείνοις, οὑτοσὶ, σαφής τε καὶ ἀληθής· ἴωμεν δ' αὖ ὡς ἐξ εἰκόνων καὶ τύπων ἐπὶ τὰ ἐμφανέστερα. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Φράσειας ἂν ἄριστα, καὶ πρός γε δὴ τούτῳ προθύμως ἰών. {ΚΥΡ.} Τὸν τοῦδε τοῦ βίου περισπασμὸν, καὶ τὴν ἐν αὐτῷ τῶν πραγμάτων πικρὰν ἀνάχυσιν καὶ ἀναφυρμὸν κατασημαίνων ἡμῖν ἀστείως ὁ Μελῳδὸς ψάλλει· «Αὕτη ἡ θάλασσα ἡ μεγάλη καὶ εὐρύχωρος. Ἐκεῖ ἑρπετὰ ὧν οὐκ ἔστιν ἀριθμὸς, ζῶα μικρὰ μετὰ μεγάλων.» Ἰχθύσι γὰρ παρεικαστέον εὖ μάλα τοὺς ἐπ' οὐδενὶ μὲν ἔσθ' ὅτε τῶν ἀναγκαίων εἰς ὄνησιν, τῇδέ τε κἀκεῖσε διᾴττοντας, καὶ μόνα συλλέγοντας τὰ ὅσαπερ ἂν ἀποφῆναι σαρκικοὺς καὶ εἰκαίους ἀνατλῆναι παρασκευάζει πόνους. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Εὖ λέγεις. {ΚΥΡ.} Ἐπιπλήττει δέ που τοῖς τοιοῖσδέ τισι καὶ ὁ τοῦ Χριστοῦ μαθητὴς, ὡδὶ λέγων· «Ἄγε δὴ νῦν οἱ λέγοντες· Σήμερον καὶ αὔριον πορευσόμεθα εἰς τήνδε τὴν πόλιν, καὶ ποιήσομεν ἐνιαυτὸν ἕνα, καὶ ἐμπορευσόμεθα, καὶ κερδήσομεν.» Καὶ μετ' ὀλίγα· «Ἀντὶ τοῦ λέγειν ὑμᾶς· Ἐὰν ὁ Κύριος θελήσῃ, καὶ
pass_a_gloss: Cyr.: [the law said] thus somehow again: 'And these you shall eat from all those in the waters: all that have fins and scales in the waters, in the seas and in the torrents, these you shall eat; and all that have neither fins nor scales in the waters, seas and torrents, of all that the waters belch forth and of every living soul in the water, it is abomination and abominations they shall be to you; from their meats you shall not eat, their carcasses you shall abhor; and all that have not fins nor scales of those in the waters, this is abomination to you.' Pall.: What the difference is in these, by spiritual contemplation, you would tell; for I do not much understand. Cyr.: Certainly; I will say, as possible, reshaping into the evident what the law took up by way of examples. Those in the waters well fashioned by the Creator of all by the law of fishes, always rowing through by the thrusts of fins, make a strong and swiftest movement wherever they choose. When the sun sends from above into the waters the warm onset of its ray, they swim up and all but dare to leap up out of the waters, refusing always to stay below, and easily get through the nets of hunters. Those not in scales and fins, i.e. in hard sheaths and clothed in a grown-on shell, least know the above, sink into the grass below always and love to haunt muddy places; powerless and easily caught, taken without sweat by those who once saw them. That is the clear and true account of them; let us go from images and types to what is more evident. Pall.: You would tell it best, going eagerly. Cyr.: The distraction of this life and the bitter overflow and confusion of affairs in it the Singer signifies wittily, singing: 'this the sea great and spacious; there creeping things without number, animals small with great'. To fishes must be likened those who sometimes dart here and there for none of the necessities toward profit, gathering only what can show them fleshly and prepares them to endure vain labors. Pall.: You speak well. Cyr.: The disciple of Christ rebukes such: 'Come now, you who say, today and tomorrow we will go into this city and make one year and trade and gain'. And after a little: 'Instead of your saying, if the Lord wills, and…'
pass_b_english: Cyril: …again, in words like these: ‘And these you shall eat of all that are in the waters: all that have fins and scales in the waters, in the seas and in the streams, these you shall eat. But all that have neither fins nor scales in the waters, in the seas and in the streams, of all that the waters bring forth and of every living creature in the water, it is an abomination, and they shall be abominations to you. You shall not eat of their flesh, and you shall abhor their carcasses. All that have neither fins nor scales, of the things in the waters, this is an abomination to you’ (Leviticus 11:9–12).
Palladius: But you yourself should explain what the difference is among these, I mean as spiritual contemplation reads them; for I hardly understand it at all.

Cyril: Certainly. I shall tell you as best I can, recasting into plain terms what the law has taken up by way of examples. Those creatures in the waters that the Creator of all has fashioned well after the pattern of fishes are always rowing their way along, as it were, by thrusting out their fins, and they move strongly and very swiftly wherever they may choose. When the sun sends the warm stroke of its rays down into the waters from above, they swim upward and all but dare to leap out of the water itself, refusing to stay below always; and they easily slip through the nets of those who hunt them. But those that are not furnished with scales and fins (those, that is, that live in hard casings and are clothed in a shell that grows with them) know almost nothing of what is above. They are always creeping down into the weeds at the bottom, and they love to linger in muddy places. They are sluggish and easily caught, and anyone who has once caught sight of them can take them without the least effort. That is the plain and true account of those creatures. Now let us go on, as from images and types, to what is clearer.
Palladius: You would do well to explain it, and to go on with it gladly.

Cyril: The Psalmist, pointing out to us with fine wit the distractions of this life and the bitter flood and confusion of affairs within it, sings: ‘This is the sea, great and wide; there are creeping things without number, living creatures small and great’ (Psalm 104:25). For we must surely liken to fishes those who at times dart this way and that for nothing needed for their good, and gather only such things as prove them fleshly and set them to endure pointless toil.

Cyril: The disciple of Christ also rebukes such people somewhere, speaking in this way: ‘Come now, you who say, “Today and tomorrow we will go into such and such a city and spend a year there, and trade and make a profit”’ (James 4:13). anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of De adoratione Book 14 exists to compare. Translated fresh from the Migne PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the withheld earlier English was not used as a base.

apparatus.note: Migne PG 68 print; the column break may cut a sentence or a word.

Opens mid-sentence: §20 ends 'Now the law has spoken' (Ἔφη τοίνυν ὁ νόμος) and §21 completes it with ὡδί πη πάλιν ('again, in words like these'). The Leviticus 11:9–12 quotation follows the LXX closely (χείμαρροι, 'streams' or 'torrents'; 'of all that the waters bring forth', ἐρεύγεται, literally 'belch forth'). 'This is the sea, great and wide…' is LXX Psalm 103:25, English Psalm 104:25; ὁ Μελῳδός ('the Singer') is David, rendered 'the Psalmist'. 'Come now, you who say…' is James 4:13 (ὁ τοῦ Χριστοῦ μαθητής, 'the disciple of Christ', is James). The section breaks inside James 4:15 ('If the Lord wills, and…'); the quotation runs on through James 4:16 in §22, so the citation is placed at its start here and should be repeated or closed in §22. In 'gather only such things as prove them fleshly and set them to endure pointless toil' the Greek (ὅσαπερ ἂν ἀποφῆναι σαρκικοὺς καὶ εἰκαίους ἀνατλῆναι παρασκευάζει πόνους) is awkward, with ἀποφῆναι left without a clear governing verb; the sense is taken as 'show them to be fleshly and prepare them to bear pointless labors'. Shellfish and other unscaled sea creatures are described as wearing a shell 'that grows with them' (συμφυές).
Palladius's question put in natural English order
Palladius's polite optative (Φράσειας ἂν ἄριστα... προθύμως ἰών): removed added condition 'especially if'; now 'You would do well to explain it, and to go on with it gladly.'
Scripture checked: Leviticus 11:9-12 LXX exact; Psalm 104:25 (LXX 103:25) exact; James 4:13 and 4:15-16 correct (quotation continues into §22)
